title: CTO Interview with Ed Plowman of Imagination Technologies
gist: Imagination Technologies CTO Ed Plowman argues the real customer problem is turning peak TOPS into delivered, predictable performance within power, thermal, memory and cost limits. He favors adaptable, programmable compute and software over hardening around today's AI workloads, citing automotive's long design cycles.

insights.claim: The biggest customer challenge is not generating more TOPS but turning those TOPS into useful work.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Peak-TOPS marketing is a weak proxy for product value; utilization matters.
insights.quote: The biggest challenge is not generating more TOPS. It is turning those TOPS into useful work.

insights.claim: Customers run graphics, computer vision, AI inference, sensor processing and conventional software simultaneously within fixed power, thermal and cost envelopes, all competing for the same resources.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Edge SoC value is set by system-level contention, not a single accelerator.

insights.claim: Memory bandwidth, data movement, utilisation, latency and software overhead can matter as much as theoretical compute capability, so datasheet peak numbers can be largely academic.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Benchmarks on peak throughput can mislead buyers of edge AI IP.
insights.quote: customers don’t ship benchmarks. They ship products.

insights.claim: Imagination optimises for delivered performance rather than benchmark performance.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Positioning against competitors that lead with peak specs.

insights.claim: Imagination favors adaptable, programmable compute over hardening around today's workload, because AI model architectures, data formats and optimisation techniques change in months while semiconductor development cycles take years.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Mismatch between AI and silicon cycles favors flexible architectures like GPUs over fixed NPUs.

insights.claim: Alternatives include tightly integrated full-stack hardware and software ecosystems, which have produced impressive results in cloud AI, and dedicated neural processing hardware, which is very efficient if the workload matches design assumptions.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Names the competing architectural approaches to edge and cloud AI compute.

insights.claim: The more specialised hardware becomes, the more certain its designers must be about the workload, and AI currently provides little such certainty.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Fixed-function AI hardware carries obsolescence risk.

insights.claim: The key design question is where to draw the line between specialisation, programmability and efficiency, and how expensive it is to move that line later.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Reframes AI hardware choice as option value.

insights.claim: Technology decisions are made years before products reach market, while an AI technique can go from research paper to deployment in months.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Customers are betting on workloads that do not yet exist.

insights.claim: In automotive, substantial validation and safety requirements, multi-year development and vehicle lifetimes well over a decade mean architectural bets are made against workloads that may not properly exist yet.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Automotive compute buyers have strong reason to demand upgradeable, flexible platforms.

insights.claim: Over-specialising too early can turn today's optimisation into tomorrow's constraint.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Supports a flexibility premium in long-life products.

themes.theme: AI's effect on strategy and software

insights.claim: Imagination no longer treats AI as a separate market; it is becoming part of almost every market served and increasingly part of graphics itself.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: GPU IP vendors fold AI into core roadmap rather than a separate NPU line.
insights.locator: How has AI changed your business

insights.claim: The bigger opportunity is often in software (compilers, tooling, workload mapping and using AI itself to optimise applications for the architecture), since software gaps cannot be bridged by simply adding engineers.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Software ecosystem is the real moat for compute IP.
insights.locator: bigger opportunity is often in software

insights.claim: Imagination's stated strategy is to build efficient, malleable hardware, invest heavily in software, and keep flexibility to move when the market moves, since the dominant workload several years out is unknowable.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman

insights.claim: AI can take repetitive analysis and optimisation work from engineers, freeing time for difficult problems requiring engineering judgement.
insights.speaker: Ed Plowman
insights.so_what: Internal AI use framed as augmentation.
